posts.title: Why the oven is lit at 04:30
posts.excerpt: At four in the morning, Spelt Yard is silent until the stones of our second-hand deck oven begin their gradual ascent to baking temperature.
posts.content:
At four-thirty in the morning, Spelt Yard is entirely still. The streetlamps cast long shadows across the cobblestones, and the tram rails along the corner of number 9 remain cold. Inside the bakehouse, however, the day begins with a single switch. Lukas Brandt turns on the heating elements of our second-hand deck oven, illuminating the stone chambers with a low hum. For nearly two hours before the first loaf enters the chamber, those heavy stone decks absorb heat. You cannot rush stone; if you load bread into a deck oven that has merely reached surface temperature, the stones lose their heat the moment cold bannetons touch them. Lighting the hearth at 04:30 is our commitment to crust, crumb, and oven spring.

While the stone warms, Lukas moves to the wooden mixing trough to begin the autolyse. We work exclusively with stoneground flours sourced from our regional milling partners. The wheat comes from Molen Ter Beke, just twenty-two kilometres away, while our dark rye arrives from Lindenhof mill, thirty-eight kilometres across the countryside. Lukas blends the stoneground flour with cool well-tempered water, leaving the mixture to rest in silence. This pause allows the grains to hydrate fully and enzymatic activity to begin naturally, long before salt or starter are introduced.

By 05:30, Ama Owusu arrives at the bench. The autolysed dough has developed strength and elasticity without aggressive mechanical mixing. Ama folds in the levain—our solitary mother culture that Tomasz Wierzbicki and Ines Moreau have fed and nurtured every single day since we opened in 2019. The room begins to smell gently of sour apple and lactic fermentation. Working with deliberate, steady movements, Ama divides the dough into 900-gram portions for our Country Sourdough, dusting the timber benches with fine rye flour before tucking each piece into wicker bannetons.

At 06:15, Ines Moreau takes her position at the oven mouth. The deck temperature has stabilized completely, holding deep radiant heat within its refractory hearth. Ines tests the dough with a fingertip, checking the gentle resistance of the ferment. With three decisive cuts of a curved razor across the proofed loaves, she transfers them to the long wooden peel and slides them smoothly onto the glowing stone floor of the deck oven. She injects steam into the sealed chamber, locking in moisture so the dough can expand freely without setting its crust prematurely. Through the thick glass door, the loaves rise dramatically, blooming along the scored ears.

Meanwhile, the subsequent bakes are already being staged. Dark rye dough, dense with whole grain from Lindenhof mill, rests in linen-lined tubs while Mei Chen prepares the buttered trays for Saturday's cardamom knot buns. Each loaf follows an unhurried sequence determined by stone deck temperatures and oven availability. Because we rely on a single oven rather than an industrial conveyor, timing is precise: bread cannot wait for the oven, and the oven cannot wait for the bread. Every morning depends on this seamless coordination between mixer, shaper, and hearth.

By seven o'clock, the transformation is complete. Priya Raman unlocks the front entrance, turning the door sign as the scent of dark caramelised wheat drifts out into Spelt Yard. The first batch of Country Sourdough rests on tall wooden cooling racks by the window, crackling softly as ambient morning air cools the crusts. The street outside begins to stir with cyclists, school children, and neighbours stopping by before work. Behind the counter, Priya stacks the day's first loaves, ready for the neighbourhood that built us. That quiet ritual at four-thirty made this bread possible.

posts.title: A week of rye from Lindenhof mill
posts.excerpt: Thirty-eight kilometres from the oven, Lindenhof mill grinds the rye that becomes our dark loaf.
posts.content:
The rye for our dark loaf arrives on Monday in paper sacks from Lindenhof mill, thirty-eight kilometres away. Tomasz checks the grind between finger and thumb before it goes into the store room, because a coarser meal drinks more water and changes the whole day.

By Tuesday the sour is built and left for thirty hours. The dough is wet, almost a paste, and it is baked in tins so that it keeps its shape. We cut the first loaf on Wednesday and it is at its best from Thursday on, when the crumb has settled.

posts.title: Cardamom buns on Saturdays
posts.excerpt: Mei shapes ninety grams of butter dough into knots with freshly ground green cardamom, Friday to Sunday.
posts.content:
From Friday to Sunday Mei shapes cardamom knot buns at the bench. The dough is a rich one with butter and milk, rolled out and spread with sugar and freshly ground green cardamom, then cut into strips and tied into knots of ninety grams each.

They go into the deck oven after the rye, at 09:30, when the heat has dropped a little. By eleven the street smells of them. They are €3.20 each, and on Saturdays they rarely last until the counter closes.

posts.title: Cooling is part of the bake
posts.excerpt: A loaf is not finished when it leaves the oven. It finishes on the rack by the window.
posts.content:
A loaf is not finished when it leaves the oven. The crumb is still setting, and the crust is still crackling as it gives off steam. We stand the loaves on the tall racks by the window and leave them alone for at least an hour.

That is why the first loaves reach the counter shelves at seven and not earlier, and why a standing order packed at eleven is always a loaf that has had its full time to cool.

posts.title: Bread for a school kitchen
posts.excerpt: Twelve seeded spelt tins a day go to Westpark Primary kitchen, packed the afternoon before.
posts.content:
Westpark Primary kitchen takes twelve seeded spelt tins a day during term time. We pack them the afternoon before, in linen-lined crates, and Hugo rides them over on the cargo bike before the cooks start slicing.

The kitchen sends the empty crates back on Friday. It is the simplest standing order we have, and one of the oldest.

posts.title: Crates on the street at 12:30
posts.excerpt: At half past twelve the cargo bike leaves Spelt Yard with the neighbours’ crates.
posts.content:
At half past twelve Hugo loads the cargo bike at the bakehouse door: baguettes for Café Lune, spelt tins for the school, rye and sourdough for Okafor Grocer on Tuesdays and Fridays. The round stays within three kilometres of Spelt Yard.

If you keep a standing order and live inside that circle, the same bike can bring your crate for €1.50 a round.
